title: Full Moon Names By Month: History and Meanings Explained
description: Discover the traditional names of every full moon of the year, from the Wolf Moon to the Cold Moon, and the fascinating history behind them.

sections.heading: The Tradition Behind Monthly Full Moon Names
paragraphs: For thousands of years, people across the globe tracked the changing seasons by naming the full moons rather than relying on standard calendar months. In North America, a blend of Native American, Colonial American, and European folklore shaped the traditional names we use today. These monikers usually reflect the shifting weather, animal behaviors, or agricultural milestones unique to that specific time of year.

While the lunar cycle takes about 29.5 days, a full moon technically occurs for only a brief moment when the Earth sits directly between the sun and the moon. Despite this, stargazers enjoy celebrating the entire night of the full moon. Exploring these traditional names offers a wonderful window into how our ancestors synchronized their daily lives with the rhythms of the natural world.

sections.heading: Winter Moons: Wolf, Snow, and Worm
paragraphs: The year kicks off in January with the Wolf Moon. Named for the howling of hungry wolves echoing through the cold winter night, this moon marks the heart of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. February brings the Snow Moon, appropriately titled due to the typically heavy snowfalls that blanket the ground during this month.

As winter begins to loosen its grip, March ushers in the Worm Moon. This name comes from the thawing ground that allows earthworm casts to appear, signaling the return of robins and other birds. It is a welcome sign that spring is finally just around the corner.

sections.heading: Spring Moons: Pink, Flower, and Strawberry
paragraphs: April features the Pink Moon, which does not actually turn a rosy shade. Instead, it is named after wild ground phlox, one of the earliest widespread spring wildflowers. May follows with the Flower Moon, celebrating the abundant blooms that emerge as late spring takes full effect across fields and forests.

June is famous for the Strawberry Moon. This name was widely used by Algonquin tribes to mark the peak of the short strawberry harvesting season. It is a sweet reminder of summer's official arrival and the bounty of fresh fruit.

sections.heading: Summer and Autumn Moons: Buck, Sturgeon, and Harvest
paragraphs: July brings us the Buck Moon, named because male deer begin to grow their new antlers around this time of year. August introduces the Sturgeon Moon, honoring the large fish that were most readily caught in the Great Lakes and other major bodies of water during late summer.

September or October often hosts the famous Harvest Moon, which is unique because it is defined by its calendar position relative to the autumn equinox rather than a specific month. The Harvest Moon rises close to sunset for several consecutive evenings, providing extra evening light that historically helped farmers gather their crops.

sections.heading: Late Year Moons: Hunter's, Beaver, and Cold
paragraphs: Following the Harvest Moon is the Hunter's Moon in October. With the fields recently cleared, hunters could easily spot animals that came out to glean remaining grains. November brings the Beaver Moon, a time when colonial trappers and Native Americans set beaver traps before the swamps and rivers froze solid.

The year concludes in December with the Cold Moon. As winter nights lengthen and temperatures plummet, this final full moon of the calendar year captures the quiet, freezing atmosphere of the darkest nights.

faq.q: Why do full moons have different names each month?
faq.a: The traditional names come from a mix of Native American, Colonial American, and European folklore. They were used to track the changing seasons, weather patterns, and agricultural activities throughout the year.

faq.q: Does the Pink Moon actually look pink?
faq.a: No, the Pink Moon does not change color. It gets its name from wild ground phlox, a pink wildflower that blooms in North America during early spring.

faq.q: What is the difference between a Harvest Moon and a regular full moon?
faq.a: The Harvest Moon is the full moon that occurs closest to the autumn equinox. It rises unusually soon after sunset for several nights in a row, providing prolonged evening light.
